experiences.title: Our Lady of Guadalupe at Tepeyac
experiences.account: Paraphrase of the Nahuatl Nican Mopohua (printed 1649): on 9-12 December 1531 the Virgin Mary appears to an Indigenous convert, Juan Diego Cuauhtlatoatzin, on the hill of Tepeyac, speaking in Nahuatl and asking that a church be built there. Bishop Juan de Zumárraga asks for a sign; Mary tells Juan Diego to gather roses blooming out of season, and when he opens his cloak (tilma) before the bishop an image of the Virgin is found imprinted on it. His uncle Juan Bernardino is also said to be healed.

primarySource.title: Nican Mopohua (attributed to Antonio Valeriano), in Luis Laso de la Vega, Huei tlamahuiçoltica (1649); Miguel Sánchez, Imagen de la Virgen María (1648)
primarySource.citation: Nican Mopohua; Sánchez 1648; 1556 inquiry of Archbishop Montúfar into the Tepeyac shrine

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: A shrine and image of Guadalupe at Tepeyac are attested by the 1550s, when the Franciscan Francisco de Bustamante preached (1556) against the devotion as encouraging idolatry, since Tepeyac had been a site associated with the Mexica mother-goddess Tonantzin. The apparition narrative itself appears in print only in 1648-49.

assessments.text: Approved devotion: the image is venerated in the most visited Marian shrine in the world, Mary is proclaimed Patroness of the Americas, and Juan Diego was canonised in 2002. The Church presents the apparition as a sign of God's closeness to Indigenous peoples amid conquest.
Generally rejects Marian apparitions as private revelation lacking scriptural warrant and sees veneration of the image as problematic, while recognising its cultural importance for Mexican identity.

Scholars disagree sharply: Stafford Poole argues there is no contemporary 16th-century evidence for the apparitions (Zumárraga's writings are silent) and that the story crystallised in the 1640s; others (e.g. defenders of the 'Escalada codex') argue for earlier oral and pictorial tradition. The image's materials and technique remain debated.

Many read Guadalupe as an inculturated gospel: Mary appears as a mestiza-looking woman speaking Nahuatl to a poor Indigenous man, challenging Spanish ecclesiastical power; critics see the devotion as also serving colonial and later nationalist ends.

debates: Historicity of Juan Diego and the 1531 apparitions (the 1996 doubts of Abbot Guillermo Schulenburg caused controversy).
Syncretism vs. inculturation (Tonantzin and Tepeyac).
Status of private revelation.
experiences.story:
Tenochtitlan, the Mexica (Aztec) capital, fell to Hernán Cortés and his Indigenous allies in 1521. A decade later the city, rebuilt as Mexico City, was the centre of New Spain. Franciscan friars had arrived in 1524 and were baptising very large numbers of Indigenous people, but the conquest had brought violence, epidemics and the destruction of the old temples. Colonial government was in turmoil: the first Audiencia (high court) under Nuño de Guzmán was notorious for abuses, and the first bishop-elect of Mexico, the Franciscan Juan de Zumárraga, clashed with it while trying to protect Indigenous people. Tepeyac, a hill north of the city, had in pre-Hispanic times been associated with a shrine to a mother goddess, often identified as Tonantzin, though the details are debated.

The best-known account of what happened there in December 1531 is the Nahuatl text called the Nican Mopohua ('Here it is told'), published in 1649 by Luis Laso de la Vega and traditionally attributed to the Indigenous scholar Antonio Valeriano (c. 1531-1605). A year earlier, in 1648, the priest Miguel Sánchez had published a Spanish account. According to these sources, on Saturday 9 December 1531, a humble Indigenous man named Juan Diego (Cuauhtlatoatzin in tradition), a recent convert, was walking to Mass at dawn when he heard birdsong on Tepeyac hill and a woman calling him by name. She appeared radiant, dressed like an Indigenous noblewoman, and identified herself as the ever-virgin Holy Mary, Mother of the true God. She asked him to go to the bishop and request that a church be built on that spot, where she would show her love and compassion to all who called on her.

Juan Diego went to Zumárraga, who listened kindly but was not convinced and told him to come back later. Returning to the hill, Juan Diego asked the Lady to send someone more important, but she insisted she had chosen him. On a second visit, the bishop asked for a sign. Meanwhile Juan Diego's uncle, Juan Bernardino, fell gravely ill, and on 12 December Juan Diego tried to go around the hill to fetch a priest for him. According to the narrative, the Lady met him, told him not to be afraid, asking whether she, his mother, was not there with him, assured him his uncle was already healed and sent him to the summit, where he found Castilian roses blooming in the December cold. He gathered them in his tilma (cloak) and carried them to the bishop.

When he opened his cloak before Zumárraga, the roses fell to the floor and on the cloth appeared the image of the Virgin as it is still venerated: a young woman with dark skin and folded hands, standing on a crescent moon, clothed with the sun's rays and a starry mantle, supported by an angel. The bishop is said to have fallen to his knees, and the uncle, according to the story, reported that the Lady had appeared to him too, healing him and giving her name as the ever-virgin Holy Mary of Guadalupe. A chapel was built at Tepeyac.

The historical record is complex. A chapel and devotion to an image of Our Lady of Guadalupe at Tepeyac are documented by the 1550s. In 1556 the Franciscan provincial Francisco de Bustamante preached against the devotion, warning it encouraged idolatry among the Indigenous, while Archbishop Alonso de Montúfar defended it, and an inquiry followed. Surviving writings of Zumárraga, who died in 1548, do not mention the apparitions, which sceptics, including some Catholic historians, see as strong evidence that the narrative developed later; defenders reply that many documents were lost and point to Indigenous annals and the oral tradition. The name Guadalupe itself recalls a famous Marian shrine in Extremadura, Spain.

Whatever its origins, the devotion grew enormously from the seventeenth century, especially among creoles (American-born Spaniards) and later among all Mexicans. Pope Benedict XIV approved a feast and office in 1754. Miguel Hidalgo carried a banner of Guadalupe at the start of the War of Independence in 1810, and she became a national symbol. In 1921 a bomb exploded near the image without damaging it, an event widely seen by devotees as providential. Juan Diego was beatified in 1990 and canonised by John Paul II in 2002, despite objections from some historians and clergy, including a former abbot of the basilica, who questioned his historical existence. The present basilica, completed in 1976, is one of the most visited Catholic shrines in the world, with millions of pilgrims around 12 December each year.

keyMoments.text: Tenochtitlan falls to Spanish and Indigenous forces, and Franciscan missionaries soon begin mass baptisms.
According to the Nican Mopohua, Juan Diego meets a radiant Lady on Tepeyac who asks for a church to be built there.
Bishop-elect Juan de Zumárraga, doubtful, asks Juan Diego for a sign.
Juan Diego gathers roses on the hill and, when he opens his tilma before the bishop, the image of the Virgin is said to appear on it.
Franciscan provincial Francisco de Bustamante preaches against the Guadalupe devotion, prompting an inquiry by Archbishop Montúfar.
Miguel Sánchez publishes the first printed account in Spanish, followed in 1649 by Laso de la Vega's Nahuatl text.
Pope Benedict XIV approves a feast and office of Our Lady of Guadalupe.
Miguel Hidalgo raises the banner of Guadalupe at the start of Mexico's War of Independence.
Pope John Paul II canonises Juan Diego despite debate about his historicity.

experiences.significance: Our Lady of Guadalupe is the most important Marian devotion in the Americas and a central symbol of Mexican and Latin American Catholic identity, embraced as a sign that the Christian God was revealed to Indigenous people in their own language and through one of their own. Her image has served as a banner of independence, social movements and Chicano identity, and the basilica draws millions of pilgrims each year. Catholic tradition sees the apparitions as a turning point in the evangelisation of Mexico; critical historians debate the narrative's origins, the silence of early sources and the extent to which it reflects later creole and Indigenous agendas, while Protestant critics object to Marian devotion itself. Anthropologists also discuss how far the devotion blended with pre-Hispanic religious patterns.

experiences.title: Pascal's 'Night of Fire' memorial
experiences.account: Quotation (French original, public domain) from the Memorial, which records an experience 'from about half past ten in the evening until about half past midnight' on Monday 23 November 1654: 'FEU. Dieu d'Abraham, Dieu d'Isaac, Dieu de Jacob, non des philosophes et des savants. Certitude. Certitude. Sentiment. Joie. Paix.' (Translation: 'FIRE. God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, not of the philosophers and scholars. Certainty. Certainty. Feeling. Joy. Peace.') It continues 'Joie, joie, joie, pleurs de joie' ('Joy, joy, joy, tears of joy').

primarySource.title: Blaise Pascal, Le Mémorial (1654)
primarySource.citation: Memorial, parchment and paper copies sewn into Pascal's coat, discovered after his death in 1662; printed in editions of the Pensées (e.g. Lafuma 913, Brunschvicg p. 142)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Pascal told no one; a servant found the text sewn into the lining of his coat after his death. The experience marked his 'second conversion', his closer association with the Jansenist community at Port-Royal, and the apologetic project that became the Pensées.

assessments.text: Read as an authentic personal encounter with the living God, though Pascal's Jansenist sympathies (condemned by Rome) make him a complex figure in Catholic memory.
Often cited as a model of personal, heart-felt faith that distinguishes the God of biblical revelation from the God of the philosophers.
The Memorial is a classic text for the contrast between rational theism and experiential faith, echoed in Pascal's line that the heart has reasons reason does not know (Pensées).
Some biographers link it to Pascal's chronic illness and a near-fatal carriage accident (an unverified story); the text itself is a rare first-hand, contemporaneous record of a mystical experience.

debates: Faith and reason: the God of Abraham vs. the God of the philosophers.
Jansenism and grace.
experiences.story:
Blaise Pascal was born in 1623 at Clermont in the Auvergne. His mother died when he was three, and his father Étienne, a tax official with strong scientific interests, educated his children himself, moving to Paris in 1631. Blaise was a prodigy: as a teenager he wrote a treatise on conic sections, and at nineteen he designed a calculating machine to help his father with tax accounts. He went on to do important work on the vacuum and on probability, the latter in correspondence with Pierre de Fermat in 1654.

Religion entered the family's life decisively in 1646, when Étienne broke his hip in Rouen and was nursed by two gentlemen influenced by Jean Duvergier de Hauranne, abbot of Saint-Cyran. Saint-Cyran was the spiritual leader of the circle associated with the convent of Port-Royal and with the theology of Cornelius Jansen, which stressed Augustine's teaching on human corruption and the absolute need for efficacious grace. The whole family experienced what historians call a 'first conversion'. Blaise's younger sister Jacqueline wanted to become a nun at Port-Royal; after their father's death in 1651 she entered in 1652, despite Blaise's initial resistance over her inheritance.

In the early 1650s Pascal moved in fashionable society and continued his scientific work. By 1654, however, he felt, as Jacqueline reported, a deep disgust with the world and yet a sense of abandonment by God. On the night of Monday 23 November 1654, from about half past ten until about half past midnight, he underwent an intense experience that he recorded at once on a sheet of paper and then copied onto a piece of parchment. The text, known as the Memorial, begins with the date, the feast of Saint Clement, and then the single word FEU, 'Fire'. It continues with the words: "Dieu d'Abraham, Dieu d'Isaac, Dieu de Jacob, non des philosophes et des savants" ('God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, not of the philosophers and the scholars'). It speaks of certainty, feeling, joy and peace, of 'the God of Jesus Christ', of 'joy, joy, joy, tears of joy', of his having separated himself from Christ, and ends with a resolve to total and sweet submission to Jesus Christ and to his spiritual director.

Pascal told no one about the document. He sewed the parchment and the paper into the lining of his coat and, according to his family, transferred it each time he changed clothes. It was found only after his death in 1662 by a servant who noticed something thick in the lining. His nephew Louis Périer made a copy; the original parchment has been lost, while the paper is preserved in the Bibliothèque nationale de France.

A later story, reported in the eighteenth century, connects the conversion with a carriage accident on the bridge at Neuilly, in which the horses plunged over the edge and Pascal was saved when the traces broke; most historians treat it as uncertain legend. What is documented is the change of life that followed. In January 1655 Pascal made a retreat at Port-Royal des Champs and put himself under the direction of Antoine Singlin. He gave up much of his worldly life, though he continued scientific and mathematical work.

From January 1656 to 1657, as the Sorbonne moved to condemn the Jansenist theologian Antoine Arnauld, Pascal wrote the eighteen anonymous Provincial Letters, a brilliant satire of Jesuit moral theology and casuistry. They were burned by order of the authorities but became classics of French prose. In March 1656 his niece Marguerite Périer, a pupil at Port-Royal, was reported cured of a lachrymal fistula after being touched with a relic said to be a thorn from Christ's crown, an event the Port-Royal circle saw as divine approval. Pascal then began notes for an apology for the Christian religion, addressed to sceptics and libertines. He died, after long illness, on 19 August 1662, aged thirty-nine; the notes were published in 1670 as the Pensées.

keyMoments.text: Blaise Pascal is born at Clermont in the Auvergne.
The Pascal family is influenced by the Jansenist circle of Saint-Cyran and Port-Royal in what is called their 'first conversion'.
Pascal's sister Jacqueline enters the convent of Port-Royal.
Between about 10:30 p.m. and 12:30 a.m. Pascal experiences the night of 'Fire' recorded in his Memorial.
He makes a retreat at Port-Royal des Champs and places himself under spiritual direction.
Pascal begins the Provincial Letters attacking Jesuit casuistry, and his niece's reported healing by the Holy Thorn strengthens his convictions.
Pascal dies in Paris, and a servant finds the Memorial sewn into his coat.
His notes for an apology for Christianity are published as the Pensées.

experiences.significance: Pascal's Memorial is one of the most famous records of a personal religious experience in Western history, and its contrast between the 'God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob' and the 'God of the philosophers' has framed debates about faith and reason ever since. The experience led to the Provincial Letters, which shaped French prose and turned public opinion against Jesuit casuistry, and to the Pensées, a classic of Christian apologetics read by Catholics, Protestants and sceptics alike. His association with Jansenism, later condemned by Rome, has made him controversial within Catholicism. Existentialist and religious thinkers, from Kierkegaard's readers to modern apologists, continue to draw on his emphasis on the heart and the limits of reason.

experiences.title: George Fox and the trembling 'Quakers'
experiences.account: From Fox's Journal (1694 edition, public domain): 'Justice Bennet of Derby was the first that called us Quakers, because I bid them tremble at the word of the Lord. This was in the year 1650.' Earlier (1647) Fox describes hearing a voice saying 'There is one, even Christ Jesus, that can speak to thy condition.' Early Friends' meetings were marked by long silence, bodily shaking and spontaneous prophetic speaking; some members went 'naked as a sign', and Fox's Book of Miracles recorded healings.

primarySource.title: George Fox, Journal (ed. Thomas Ellwood, 1694)
primarySource.citation: Journal, 1647 and 1650 entries; Fox, Book of Miracles (reconstructed by H.J. Cadbury, 1948)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Opponents mocked the trembling as madness or demonic possession; Puritan authorities feared the Quakers' claim of an Inner Light superior to Scripture and clergy. James Nayler's 1656 re-enactment of Christ's entry into Jerusalem at Bristol led to his brutal punishment and pushed Friends toward greater discipline.

assessments.text: Trembling expressed the awe of being searched by the Light of Christ within; modern Friends mostly practise silent waiting worship and see the early phenomena as a historic intensity of the same Spirit.
Puritan critics such as John Owen judged the Quaker Inner Light a dangerous subordination of Scripture to subjective experience; many Reformed writers still class early Quakerism with 'enthusiasm'.
Some see early Friends as forerunners of Spirit-led worship and bodily manifestations, though Quaker theology differs widely from Pentecostalism.
Rosemary Moore and others show the movement's radical Civil War context; Fox's Journal was edited after his death, and his miracle book was largely suppressed by later Friends.

debates: Inner Light vs. sufficiency of Scripture.
'Enthusiasm' and public order in Restoration England.
experiences.story:
England in the 1640s and 1650s was in upheaval. Civil war between King and Parliament, the execution of Charles I in 1649 and the collapse of the Church of England's bishops and prayer book left the field open to an extraordinary variety of religious groups: Presbyterians, Independents, Baptists, Fifth Monarchists, Ranters and many 'Seekers' who had left all churches and waited for a new outpouring of apostolic power. Into this world came George Fox, born in 1624 at Drayton-in-the-Clay (now Fenny Drayton), Leicestershire, the son of a Puritan weaver.

Fox was apprenticed to a shoemaker and grazier, but at nineteen, troubled by the hypocrisy he saw in professing Christians, he left home and wandered for several years, seeking out priests and preachers who, he felt, could not help him. In his Journal, dictated later in life and published in 1694, he describes the turning point in 1647: when all his hopes in people were gone, he heard a voice which said, "There is one, even Christ Jesus, that can speak to thy condition," and his heart leapt for joy. He came to teach that Christ the inward Light enlightens every person, that true worship needs no 'steeple-houses', paid ministers or outward sacraments, and that believers could be freed from sin in this life.

Fox began preaching around the Midlands in 1647-1648, often interrupting church services after the sermon to challenge the minister, which was legal in some circumstances but provocative. Early hearers and followers, who called themselves 'Children of the Light' or 'Friends of the Truth', frequently experienced bodily shaking and trembling in their meetings, sometimes with groaning, weeping or falling. They understood this as the power of God working on the soul, in line with biblical texts about trembling at God's word (Isaiah 66:2, 5). Opponents found it alarming and theatrical.

In October 1650 Fox spoke at a meeting at Derby and was arrested and brought before the magistrates, Gervase Bennet and Nathaniel Barton. Charged under the Blasphemy Act of 1650, apparently for claiming to be free of sin, he was imprisoned for about a year. According to his Journal, it was Justice Bennet who first called them 'Quakers', because Fox told him to tremble at the word of the Lord. The nickname, meant as mockery, stuck and was eventually adopted by the movement itself, though its formal name became the Religious Society of Friends.

After his release Fox travelled north. In 1652 he climbed Pendle Hill in Lancashire and, he wrote, saw in a vision a great people to be gathered. Soon after he preached to about a thousand Seekers on Firbank Fell in Westmorland, many of whom joined him, and at Swarthmoor Hall he converted Margaret Fell, wife of a judge, whose home became the movement's centre; she later married Fox. Itinerant preachers, the 'Valiant Sixty', including many women, spread the message across England, Ireland, Wales and beyond, and by 1660 there were perhaps 35,000 to 60,000 Quakers.

Their behaviour shocked many contemporaries. They refused to doff hats to social superiors, used 'thee' and 'thou' to everyone, refused to swear oaths or pay tithes, and occasionally performed prophetic signs, such as going 'naked as a sign'. In 1656 James Nayler, a leading Quaker preacher, rode into Bristol in a re-enactment of Christ's entry into Jerusalem, with followers singing hosanna; Parliament had him whipped, branded and his tongue bored. Many Quakers were imprisoned, and after the Restoration of 1660 laws against nonconformist worship hit them hard; thousands were jailed and hundreds died in prison.

The movement gradually became more orderly. The 1660 declaration to Charles II articulated the peace testimony; Fox organised monthly and quarterly meetings; Robert Barclay's Apology (1676) set out Quaker theology systematically; and William Penn founded Pennsylvania in 1681 as a 'holy experiment' in religious liberty. After the Toleration Act of 1689, Quakers became known more for quiet, silent worship than for trembling. Fox died in London in 1691.

keyMoments.text: George Fox is born at Drayton-in-the-Clay, Leicestershire, to a Puritan weaver's family.
After years of seeking, Fox records hearing that 'Christ Jesus' alone could speak to his condition, and he begins to preach.
Groups of 'Children of the Light' gather around Fox, and trembling and shaking are reported in their meetings.
Fox is imprisoned at Derby for blasphemy, and Justice Gervase Bennet nicknames his followers 'Quakers'.
Fox's vision on Pendle Hill and preaching on Firbank Fell launch the movement in northern England, centred at Swarthmoor Hall.
James Nayler's symbolic entry into Bristol leads to his savage punishment by Parliament.
Quakers issue a declaration of their peace testimony to Charles II amid widespread persecution.
The Toleration Act grants Quakers and other dissenters freedom of worship in England.

experiences.significance: The early Quaker movement was one of the most radical outgrowths of the English Revolution, and its emphasis on the inward Light, unprogrammed worship, equality of men and women in ministry and refusal of oaths and violence left a lasting mark. Quakers became pioneers in religious liberty (Pennsylvania), prison reform, the abolition of slavery, peace work and relief agencies, and the Society of Friends remains a small but influential tradition worldwide, especially in East Africa. Their trembling worship is an early modern example of bodily experiences of the Spirit that later revival and Pentecostal movements would echo. Critics from Puritan to modern evangelical writers have questioned the inward Light's relation to Scripture and the Quakers' rejection of outward sacraments.

experiences.title: The prophets of the Cévennes (Camisards)
experiences.account: Paraphrase of the testimonies collected in Le Théâtre sacré des Cévennes (London, 1707): after Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes (1685), Huguenot peasants in the Cévennes, often children and young people, began to fall to the ground, shake and convulse, then speak prophecies in good French (rather than their Occitan dialect) calling for repentance and resistance to 'Babylon'. The movement fed the Camisard revolt (1702-1704/5); refugee 'French Prophets' later caused a sensation in London (1706 onwards).

primarySource.title: Le Théâtre sacré des Cévennes (ed. Maximilien Misson, 1707); English trans. A Cry from the Desart (1707)
primarySource.citation: Théâtre sacré des Cévennes, testimonies of eyewitnesses

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Catholic authorities treated the prophets as fanatics and rebels; many exiled Reformed pastors (e.g. in Geneva and London) were also embarrassed and disowned them. In England the French Prophets attracted followers and were mocked as 'enthusiasts'; some later influenced the Shakers.

assessments.text: Remembered as a desperate witness of a persecuted 'Church of the Desert'; Reformed theology, which is largely cessationist, has been ambivalent about the prophetic phenomena while honouring the martyrs.
Historically condemned as rebellious fanaticism; today Catholic historians also recognise the brutality of the dragonnades and the war.
Some historians of Pentecostalism list the Camisards among pre-modern 'charismatic' movements showing prophecy and bodily manifestations under persecution.
Clarke Garrett and others analyse the phenomena as a form of spirit possession and popular religion under extreme stress; contemporary Catholic doctors also tried to explain them medically.

debates: Prophecy and violence: the link to armed rebellion.
Embarrassment of mainstream Reformed churches toward ecstatic prophecy.
experiences.story:
In October 1685 King Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes, which since 1598 had given French Protestants (Huguenots) limited legal toleration. Protestant worship was banned, pastors were ordered to leave the kingdom within fifteen days, churches were demolished and lay people were forbidden to emigrate. Many had already been forced to convert by the dragonnades, the billeting of soldiers in Protestant homes. In the mountainous Cévennes and Vivarais of southern France, where Reformed Protestantism was deeply rooted among peasants and artisans, communities lost their pastors overnight and many professed Catholicism outwardly while continuing to pray and sing psalms in secret.

In this situation of repression and leaderlessness, prophetic phenomena broke out. Beginning in 1688 in the Dauphiné, a young shepherdess, Isabeau Vincent, began to speak in her sleep, preaching repentance and denouncing the Mass; she drew large crowds before being arrested. Similar 'inspirés' (inspired ones) appeared in the Vivarais and then the Cévennes: men, women and many children who fell to the ground, trembled and shook with agitations, and then spoke in fluent French, rather than their everyday Occitan dialect, calling for repentance, announcing the fall of 'Babylon' (the Catholic Church) and promising deliverance. Clandestine open-air assemblies, the 'Assemblies of the Desert', gathered in woods and ravines, and preachers such as Claude Brousson, a lawyer turned minister, travelled in secret until his execution in 1698.

The authorities responded with soldiers, imprisonment, the galleys and executions. The tension culminated in July 1702 at Le Pont-de-Montvert, a village in the Cévennes. The Abbé François de Langlade du Chayla, inspector of missions, was holding Protestants prisoner in his house there. On the night of 24 July 1702 a group of armed Protestants led by the prophet Abraham Mazel and Pierre Esprit Séguier attacked the house, freed the prisoners and killed the abbé. This marked the beginning of the Camisard war, named possibly from the white shirts (camisa in Occitan) the rebels wore.

For two years several thousand Camisard fighters waged a guerrilla war against tens of thousands of royal troops. Their leaders, notably Pierre Laporte, known as Roland, and Jean Cavalier, a young baker's apprentice, were guided in part by prophets who, according to Camisard testimonies, discerned traitors, chose targets and gave orders while in ecstatic states. Royal forces under Marshal Montrevel burned hundreds of villages in the Upper Cévennes. In 1704 Marshal Villars combined force with negotiation; Cavalier made terms in May 1704 and left France, eventually serving the British army and becoming lieutenant-governor of Jersey. Roland was killed in August 1704, and the revolt dwindled, though sporadic fighting continued for years.

Contemporary judgements were deeply divided. Catholic writers such as Esprit Fléchier, bishop of Nîmes, described the prophets as fanatics and the result of deliberate training of children by agitators. Some Protestant pastors in exile, such as Pierre Jurieu, who had predicted the imminent fall of the papacy, were sympathetic; others, like many Huguenot refugees in London and Geneva, were embarrassed. In 1706 several Camisard prophets arrived in London, where as the 'French Prophets' they attracted English followers and controversy. In 1707 Maximilien Misson published Le Théâtre sacré des Cévennes, a collection of sworn testimonies by refugees describing the phenomena.

After the war, Antoine Court reorganised the underground Reformed church from 1715 on a more orderly basis, explicitly distancing it from prophetic inspiration. French Protestants regained civil status in 1787 under the Edict of Toleration. The Camisards remain a powerful memory in the Cévennes, where an annual gathering is held at the Musée du Désert at Mialet.

keyMoments.text: Louis XIV revokes the Edict of Nantes, banning Protestant worship and exiling Reformed pastors.
The shepherdess Isabeau Vincent begins prophesying in the Dauphiné, and 'inspired' prophets appear in the Vivarais and Cévennes.
The underground preacher Claude Brousson is executed at Montpellier.
Armed Protestants led by prophets kill the Abbé du Chayla at Le Pont-de-Montvert, starting the Camisard war.
Royal troops under Marshal Montrevel burn hundreds of villages in the Upper Cévennes.
Jean Cavalier makes terms with Marshal Villars and leaves France; Roland is killed in August.
Exiled Camisard prophets arrive in London, where they become known as the 'French Prophets'.
Antoine Court begins reorganising the clandestine French Reformed church on non-prophetic lines.

experiences.significance: The Camisard prophets show how intense religious repression could produce mass prophetic and ecstatic phenomena, and how such experiences could fuel armed resistance. They influenced the 'French Prophets' in England, who in turn affected early Methodism's debates over enthusiasm and possibly the origins of the Shakers through Jane and James Wardley's circle. For French Protestants they remain heroes of conscience and resistance, while Catholic critics saw them as fanatics and rebels, and modern historians study them as a case of prophecy, violence and popular religion under persecution. Pentecostal and charismatic historians sometimes cite them as early modern precursors of tongues and prophecy.

experiences.title: The Moravian 'Pentecost' at Herrnhut
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Moravian accounts: the refugee community at Herrnhut, divided by disputes, signed a 'Brotherly Agreement' in May 1727; on 13 August 1727, at a communion service in the Lutheran parish church at Berthelsdorf, participants reported an overwhelming sense of the Spirit's presence, reconciliation and love. Shortly afterward a round-the-clock prayer watch began, said to have continued for about a hundred years, and from 1732 Moravian missionaries went to the Caribbean, Greenland and beyond.

primarySource.title: Moravian Church memoirs and Zinzendorf's later recollections
primarySource.citation: Herrnhut Diary, August 1727; accounts collected in Moravian histories

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Zinzendorf and the Brethren regarded 13 August as the spiritual birthday of the Renewed Unity of the Brethren. The experience was quiet and communal rather than ecstatic.

assessments.text: Celebrated annually as the renewal of the Unitas Fratrum; it shaped a heart-religion centred on the wounds of Christ and missionary zeal.
Moravians directly influenced John Wesley (on the voyage to Georgia and in London), so Herrnhut is seen as one root of the Evangelical Revival.
The 24-hour prayer watch is a model for modern prayer movements (e.g. 24-7 Prayer).
W.R. Ward places Herrnhut within a wider Central European Protestant awakening driven by persecution, migration and Pietism.

debates: Emotional 'heart religion' and its critics in Lutheran orthodoxy.
Later Moravian 'Sifting Time' excesses in the 1740s.
experiences.story:
The Unitas Fratrum, or Unity of the Brethren, grew out of the Hussite movement in fifteenth-century Bohemia and Moravia. After the Habsburg victory at the White Mountain in 1620 it was suppressed, and its last bishop, Jan Amos Comenius, died in exile in 1670. Small groups of secret Protestants survived in Moravia. In 1722 a carpenter named Christian David led a few such families across the border to Saxony, where Count Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf, a young Lutheran nobleman shaped by Pietism at Halle, allowed them to settle on his estate at Berthelsdorf. They founded a village on the road to Zittau beneath a hill called the Hutberg, which they named Herrnhut, 'under the Lord's watch'.

Over the next few years Herrnhut attracted not only Moravian refugees but also Lutheran Pietists, Reformed and other seekers. Diversity brought conflict. A charismatic member, Johann Andreas Krüger, accused the Lutheran parish church of Berthelsdorf of being Babylon, and disputes over doctrine, church order and the Count's authority threatened to split the community by 1726-1727. Zinzendorf, who held a position at the Saxon court in Dresden, took leave to live at Herrnhut and devote himself to reconciling the settlers.

He visited homes, studied with the residents the old order of the Unity of the Brethren in Comenius' account, and on 12 May 1727 the community agreed to a set of 'Manorial Injunctions and Prohibitions' together with a 'Brotherly Agreement' (the Statutes) setting out rules for common life. Small groups ('bands') were formed for mutual confession and prayer. The summer of 1727 brought, according to Moravian accounts, a growing sense of spiritual renewal: people met to pray at night, and on 5 August Zinzendorf spent the night in prayer and conversation with a group of men on the Hutberg.

On Wednesday 13 August 1727 the community went to the Berthelsdorf parish church for a service of confession and the Lord's Supper, led by the Lutheran pastor Johann Andreas Rothe. According to the accounts of participants, recorded in Moravian sources and later retold by Zinzendorf and others, during the service the whole congregation was overcome by a deep sense of God's presence, of forgiveness and of unity; former opponents embraced, and many wept. Zinzendorf later described the day as a true outpouring of the Holy Spirit, and the Moravians came to regard it as their spiritual birthday, the 'Moravian Pentecost'. Around the same time, children in the community, especially girls, were reported to have experienced intense religious awakening.

Practical consequences followed quickly. On 27 August 1727 twenty-four men and twenty-four women agreed to take turns praying, one hour each, so that prayer would continue around the clock. According to Moravian tradition, this 'hourly intercession' continued without interruption for about a century. From 1728 the community received a daily 'watchword' (Losung), and from 1731 the printed Daily Texts (Losungen), still published today in dozens of languages.

The renewal soon turned outward. In 1731, at the coronation of Christian VI in Copenhagen, Zinzendorf met Anton, an enslaved man from the Danish West Indies, who spoke of the people there who had never heard the gospel. In 1732 Leonard Dober and David Nitschmann sailed for St Thomas, the first Moravian missionaries; others soon went to Greenland, Suriname, Georgia, South Africa and many other places. Herrnhut had only a few hundred inhabitants, but within decades it had sent out hundreds of missionaries. Moravian missionaries on the voyage to Georgia in 1735-1736 deeply impressed John Wesley, and the Moravian Peter Böhler guided him before his Aldersgate experience. Critics, including Lutheran authorities in Saxony and later Wesley himself, objected to Zinzendorf's sentimental 'blood and wounds' theology and to excesses of the 1740s known as the 'Sifting Time'.

keyMoments.text: Moravian refugees led by Christian David settle on Count Zinzendorf's estate and found Herrnhut.
Doctrinal and personal disputes threaten to divide the mixed community at Herrnhut.
The community agrees to the Brotherly Agreement setting out rules for common life.
At a Communion service in Berthelsdorf church the congregation experiences what it called an outpouring of the Spirit and reconciliation.
Forty-eight members begin the round-the-clock 'hourly intercession', said to have continued for about a century.
The first printed Daily Texts (Losungen) are published for the community.
Leonard Dober and David Nitschmann sail for St Thomas, launching Moravian missions worldwide.
Moravians on the voyage to Georgia impress John Wesley, an influence that leads toward his Aldersgate experience.

experiences.significance: The Herrnhut renewal of 1727 transformed a divided refugee settlement into the Renewed Moravian Church, one of the pioneers of Protestant world mission, decades before the better-known missionary societies of the 1790s. Its stress on heart religion, small groups, continuous prayer and daily texts influenced Wesley and the Methodist movement, Pietism and later evangelicalism, and the 24-hour prayer model has been revived by modern movements such as 24-7 Prayer. Lutheran critics and others objected to Zinzendorf's theology and to the community's emotional excesses during the 'Sifting Time', and historians note the idealisation of 13 August in later Moravian memory. The Moravian Church today has a large majority of its members in Africa and the Caribbean.

experiences.title: Jonathan Edwards and the Northampton awakening
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Edwards' A Faithful Narrative of the Surprising Work of God (1737): from late 1734, after sermons on justification by faith, religious concern spread through Northampton until 'scarcely a single person in the whole town' was unconcerned about eternal things; Edwards estimated more than 300 conversions in six months, describing cases such as the dying Abigail Hutchinson and four-year-old Phebe Bartlet. The revival waned after his uncle Joseph Hawley took his own life (1735). In 1740-42, with George Whitefield's preaching, outcries, fainting and convulsions became common.

primarySource.title: Jonathan Edwards, A Faithful Narrative (1737); The Distinguishing Marks of a Work of the Spirit of God (1741); Religious Affections (1746)
primarySource.citation: Faithful Narrative; Distinguishing Marks; Religious Affections, Part III

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Edwards defended the revival against critics like Charles Chauncy (Seasonable Thoughts, 1743), who saw 'enthusiasm' and disorder; yet Edwards also argued that bodily effects and strong emotions prove nothing either way, and that true 'religious affections' are known by their fruit in holiness.

assessments.text: Edwards' discernment framework (Distinguishing Marks, Religious Affections) is still the classic Reformed guide: revival is a sovereign work of God, but manifestations must be tested by Scripture and fruit.
Even cessationists generally accept the Awakening as genuine revival, distinguishing it from claims of new revelation or miraculous gifts.
Charismatic leaders (e.g. during the Toronto Blessing) cited Edwards to defend falling and outcries, a use that Reformed critics contest.
Thomas Kidd and others show a transatlantic revival network; contemporaries split into 'New Lights' and 'Old Lights'. Edwards was dismissed by his church in 1750 over communion qualifications.

debates: Bodily manifestations as evidence (Edwards: neither proof nor disproof).
Old Lights vs. New Lights; 'enthusiasm'.
Suicide and religious melancholy during revival.
experiences.story:
Northampton was a prosperous farming town on the Connecticut River in western Massachusetts, a Congregationalist community founded in 1654. For nearly sixty years its pastor had been Solomon Stoddard, a powerful preacher who had presided over several local revivals or 'harvests' and had controversially opened the Lord's Supper to all morally upright church members as a 'converting ordinance'. In 1727 his grandson Jonathan Edwards, born in 1703 and educated at Yale, became his assistant, and on Stoddard's death in 1729 the sole pastor of one of the largest and most influential churches in the colony.

Edwards later wrote that he found the town in a period of 'dullness in religion'. In his account, young people were given to 'night walking', frequenting the tavern and 'lewd practices', and the town was divided by party quarrels. In 1733 he noticed a change among the young, who began to accept his advice to give up evening frolics. In the spring of 1734 the sudden deaths of a young man and a young married woman deeply affected the town.

In late 1734 Edwards preached a series of sermons on justification by faith alone, in response to what he saw as a creeping Arminianism in New England that made salvation depend partly on human effort. Then, as he recounted, a young woman known as one of the 'greatest company-keepers' in town came to him in deep concern and, he believed, experienced true conversion. Her change, he wrote, struck like a flash of lightning on the hearts of the young people. Over the following months religious concern spread throughout the town; by his account there was scarcely a person, old or young, who was unconcerned about eternal things.

Edwards estimated that in the spring and summer of 1735 more than three hundred people in Northampton were converted, and that the town 'seemed to be full of the presence of God'. Families were full of joy, worship was transformed and business was neglected for religious meetings. He interviewed many people and described their experiences in detail: conviction of sin, fear of hell, a sense of God's sovereign justice, and then a new sense of the excellency of Christ and of God's grace. He recorded two case studies at length: Abigail Hutchinson, a young woman who died during the revival after a deep experience of peace, and Phebe Bartlet, a girl of four whose devotion astonished her parents. Similar awakenings occurred in about two dozen other towns along the Connecticut valley.

The revival ended abruptly. On 1 June 1735 Joseph Hawley, Edwards' uncle by marriage and a respected townsman, in deep spiritual despair, cut his own throat. Edwards reported that after this many people felt urged by a strange impulse to do the same, and that the intensity of the awakening began to decline. He interpreted these events as Satan's work.

Edwards described the revival in a long letter to the Boston minister Benjamin Colman, which was published in London in 1737 with a preface by Isaac Watts and John Guyse as A Faithful Narrative of the Surprising Work of God in the Conversion of Many Hundred Souls in Northampton. It was read on both sides of the Atlantic, including by John Wesley, and helped make revival a recognised category in Protestant life. In 1740 George Whitefield's preaching tour reached Northampton, where Edwards wept during his sermons, and a much wider awakening followed; Edwards preached 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God' at Enfield, Connecticut, in July 1741.

The wider awakening generated controversy. Critics such as Charles Chauncy of Boston attacked its emotional excesses, while some radical revivalists, such as James Davenport, divided churches. Edwards defended genuine revival but tried to discern true from false religious experience in works such as The Distinguishing Marks (1741) and A Treatise Concerning Religious Affections (1746). In 1750, after a dispute about restricting communion to those who professed conversion, his congregation dismissed him.

keyMoments.text: Jonathan Edwards succeeds his grandfather Solomon Stoddard as pastor of the Northampton church.
Edwards preaches a series of sermons on justification by faith alone amid concern about Arminianism.
The conversion of a young woman known for worldliness sparks widespread religious concern among Northampton's youth.
During spring and summer Edwards counts more than three hundred conversions, and revival spreads to some two dozen Connecticut valley towns.
Joseph Hawley's suicide marks the beginning of the revival's decline.
Edwards' Faithful Narrative of the Surprising Work of God is published in London with a preface by Isaac Watts and John Guyse.
George Whitefield preaches at Northampton, and the Great Awakening spreads across New England.
Edwards publishes Religious Affections, his major attempt to distinguish genuine from false religious experience.

experiences.significance: The Northampton revival was the prelude to the First Great Awakening, and Edwards' Faithful Narrative became the template for how evangelical Protestants describe, expect and evaluate revival. His careful analysis of conversion and his later works on religious affections remain foundational for evangelical and Reformed thinking on religious experience, and Edwards is widely regarded as America's greatest colonial theologian. Critics then and since, from Charles Chauncy to modern historians, have questioned the emotional pressure, the fear of hell and the psychological effects of revival, as the Hawley suicide tragically illustrated. Historians also debate how far published narratives such as Edwards' helped create the very revivals they described.

experiences.title: Wesley's heart 'strangely warmed' at Aldersgate
experiences.account: From John Wesley's Journal, 24 May 1738 (public domain): 'In the evening I went very unwillingly to a society in Aldersgate Street, where one was reading Luther's preface to the Epistle to the Romans. About a quarter before nine, while he was describing the change which God works in the heart through faith in Christ, I felt my heart strangely warmed. I felt I did trust in Christ, Christ alone, for salvation; and an assurance was given me that He had taken away my sins, even mine, and saved me from the law of sin and death.' On 1 January 1739, at a Fetter Lane love feast, Wesley records that 'the power of God came mightily upon us', many crying out for joy and falling to the ground.
experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Wesley, influenced by the Moravian Peter Böhler, interpreted the experience as receiving the assurance of saving faith. His brother Charles had a similar experience three days earlier. In Wesley's field-preaching from 1739, hearers often cried out, convulsed or fell; Wesley generally regarded this as God's work mixed with natural and sometimes diabolical elements.

assessments.text: Aldersgate Day (24 May) is commemorated; the experience grounds the Methodist doctrine of assurance, though historians and Methodist theologians debate whether it was Wesley's 'conversion' or one stage in a longer journey.
Wesley remained an Anglican priest; contemporary bishops worried about 'enthusiasm' and the irregularity of field-preaching.
Wesley's account of people falling under the power of God is often cited as a historical precedent for being 'slain in the Spirit'.
Henry Rack shows Wesley's later journals rarely mention Aldersgate and that his spiritual doubts continued; the episode gained iconic status largely in 19th-century Methodism.

debates: Assurance of salvation: normative or occasional?
Was Aldersgate Wesley's conversion?
Enthusiasm and bodily manifestations in early Methodism.
experiences.story:
John Wesley was born in 1703 at Epworth, Lincolnshire, the fifteenth child of Samuel Wesley, a High Church Anglican rector, and Susanna Wesley, a strong-minded and devout mother. Rescued as a small child from a fire at the rectory in 1709, he was later described by his mother as a 'brand plucked from the burning'. At Oxford, where he became a fellow of Lincoln College, he and his brother Charles led a small group of earnest students, mocked as the 'Holy Club' and 'Methodists' for their methodical rule of prayer, fasting, frequent communion, Bible study and visits to prisoners.

In October 1735 John and Charles sailed as missionaries to the new colony of Georgia. On the voyage a terrible storm terrified the English passengers, but a group of German Moravians sang psalms calmly throughout. Wesley noted in his journal that he asked one whether he was not afraid and was told no, not even the women and children. In Georgia, the Moravian leader August Gottlieb Spangenberg asked him whether he knew Jesus Christ and had the witness of the Spirit within himself, questions Wesley could answer only uncertainly. His ministry in Savannah was a failure: his strict High Church practice antagonised parishioners, and after a failed romance with Sophia Hopkey and a legal dispute when he refused her communion, he left in December 1737.

Back in England in February 1738, he wrote that he had gone to America to convert the Indians, but who would convert him? He met the young Moravian Peter Böhler, who persuaded him that true faith brings instant forgiveness, assurance and peace, and that he lacked it. Böhler advised him to 'preach faith till you have it; and then, because you have it, you will preach faith'. On Whitsunday, 21 May 1738, Charles, ill in bed, experienced assurance of forgiveness and wrote in his journal of finding peace with God.

Three days later, on Wednesday 24 May 1738, John records that he opened his Bible at five in the morning on the words that he was not far from the kingdom of God, and in the afternoon heard the anthem at St Paul's Cathedral, 'Out of the deep have I called unto thee, O Lord'. His journal continues: "In the evening I went very unwillingly to a society in Aldersgate Street, where one was reading Luther's preface to the Epistle to the Romans. About a quarter before nine, while he was describing the change which God works in the heart through faith in Christ, I felt my heart strangely warmed. I felt I did trust in Christ, Christ alone, for salvation; and an assurance was given me that he had taken away my sins, even mine, and saved me from the law of sin and death." He prayed for those who had mistreated him and testified to everyone there, and was then taken by friends to Charles, who greeted him with the hymn he had just written.

Wesley's journal shows that doubts and temptations returned in the following months, and he even wrote at times that he was not a Christian. In the summer of 1738 he visited Herrnhut and met Zinzendorf. On 1 January 1739, at a love feast at the Fetter Lane Society in London with the Wesleys, George Whitefield and others, he reported that about three in the morning the power of God came on them mightily, so that many cried out for joy and fell to the ground. In April 1739, at Whitefield's urging, he overcame his scruples and preached in the open air near Bristol to some three thousand people. From then until his death in 1791 he travelled about 250,000 miles on horseback, preaching perhaps 40,000 sermons and organising converts into societies, classes and bands within the Church of England.

Interpretations of Aldersgate differ. Methodist tradition has often treated it as Wesley's evangelical conversion; others, noting his earlier devotion and later doubts, see it as one stage in a longer process of assurance and a turning point in his preaching. Wesley himself rarely referred to the date afterwards. It is nonetheless commemorated each year by Methodists as 'Aldersgate Day', and a memorial near the site in the City of London marks the event.

keyMoments.text: John Wesley is born at Epworth rectory, Lincolnshire.
At Oxford John and Charles Wesley lead the 'Holy Club', mocked as 'Methodists'.
On the voyage to Georgia Wesley is struck by the calm faith of Moravians during a storm, and Spangenberg questions him about assurance.
Back in England after a failed mission, Wesley meets Peter Böhler, who urges him to seek saving faith.
Charles Wesley experiences assurance of forgiveness on Whitsunday.
At a society meeting in Aldersgate Street, during the reading of Luther's preface to Romans, John Wesley feels his 'heart strangely warmed'.
At the Fetter Lane love feast, Wesley reports the power of God coming mightily on those present.
Wesley begins open-air preaching near Bristol, launching the Methodist revival.

experiences.significance: Aldersgate became the defining moment in Methodist memory and a classic statement of evangelical assurance of salvation by faith. The movement that followed, Methodism, grew into a worldwide family of churches, gave rise to the Holiness and, indirectly, Pentecostal movements, and helped shape evangelical Christianity and social reform in Britain and America. Wesley's teaching on assurance and Christian perfection was criticised by Calvinists such as Whitefield and by Anglican authorities as 'enthusiasm', and scholars still debate whether Aldersgate was a conversion or one step in a longer journey. It also shows the influence of Luther and the Moravians on English religion.

experiences.title: Cane Ridge camp meeting: falling, jerks and holy laughter

place.name: Cane Ridge Meeting House, Bourbon County, Kentucky

experiences.account: Paraphrase of Barton W. Stone's autobiography and contemporary letters: at a Presbyterian sacramental gathering on 6-12 August 1801, attended by an estimated 10,000-20,000 people with Presbyterian, Methodist and Baptist preachers speaking from several stands at once, many fell to the ground and lay helpless for hours. Stone lists 'exercises': the falling exercise, the jerks (violent jerking of head and body), the dancing, barking, laughing, running and singing exercises.

primarySource.title: Barton W. Stone, A Short History of the Life of Barton W. Stone, Written by Himself (1847)
primarySource.citation: Stone, Autobiography, ch. 'The Great Revival'; letters published in contemporary religious magazines

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Supporters saw an American Pentecost; critics in the Presbyterian Synod of Kentucky saw disorder and doctrinal laxity. The revival contributed to the Cumberland Presbyterian and Stone-Campbell (Christian Church/Disciples) splits and fuelled the Methodist and Baptist camp-meeting tradition.

assessments.text: Remembered as a foundational frontier revival; Stone himself later grew more cautious, judging some exercises genuine and others the result of excitement or imitation.
Often regarded as an example of revivalism that confused emotion with grace and weakened confessional order.
Cited as a precedent for falling, shaking and laughter in modern revivals such as Toronto (1994).

Paul Conkin calls it 'America's Pentecost'; historians emphasise sacramental-season roots in Scottish Presbyterianism, crowd dynamics and frontier social life; Ann Taves traces how such 'fits and trances' were interpreted religiously and medically.

debates: Emotionalism and crowd contagion.
Revivalism vs. confessional order.
Interpreting bodily 'exercises'.
experiences.story:
At the end of the eighteenth century Kentucky was a raw frontier, admitted as a state only in 1792. Settlers from Virginia, the Carolinas and Pennsylvania lived scattered across the countryside with few churches, and ministers complained of irreligion, drunkenness and violence. Presbyterians, many of Scots-Irish background, kept the old Scottish custom of 'sacramental seasons' or 'holy fairs': multi-day communion gatherings with preaching, fasting, self-examination and the Lord's Supper, which in Scotland had sometimes become occasions of revival.

In 1800 James McGready, a Presbyterian minister in Logan County in south-western Kentucky, led communion seasons at the Red River and Gasper River meeting houses where people fell to the ground, cried out and professed conversion. Because people came from long distances and camped on the grounds in wagons and tents, these gatherings became known as camp meetings. In the spring of 1801 Barton W. Stone, the young Presbyterian pastor of the Cane Ridge and Concord congregations in Bourbon County, near Paris in central Kentucky, travelled to Logan County to see the revivals for himself and returned deeply impressed. Revival spread through central Kentucky that summer.

Stone arranged a communion season at the Cane Ridge meeting house, a log church built in 1791, beginning on Friday 6 August 1801. Contemporary estimates of the crowd ranged from about 10,000 to 25,000 people, at a time when the largest town in the state, Lexington, had fewer than 2,000 inhabitants. Presbyterian, Methodist and some Baptist ministers preached simultaneously from stands and wagons in different parts of the grounds, day and night, for about six days. Over a thousand people are said to have received communion.

Eyewitnesses, including Stone himself in his later autobiography and several letters published at the time, described extraordinary bodily 'exercises'. People fell to the ground, sometimes lying unconscious for hours: the 'falling exercise'. Others experienced 'the jerks', violent involuntary twitching of the head and body; some danced, ran, laughed uncontrollably or, according to some reports, made barking sounds. Many cried out for mercy and then shouted for joy at conversion. One Presbyterian minister estimated that some three thousand people fell during the meeting. Critics also reported drinking, disorder and sexual misbehaviour on the fringes of the encampment, though defenders thought such reports exaggerated.

Reactions were sharply divided. Supporters saw the meeting as an outpouring of the Holy Spirit comparable to Pentecost. Many Presbyterian leaders were alarmed by the disorder, by the cooperation with Methodists and by the revivalists' tendency to downplay Calvinist doctrines of predestination in favour of a universal call to repent. In 1803 Stone and four other ministers withdrew from the Synod of Kentucky and formed the independent Springfield Presbytery; in June 1804 they dissolved it in a document called 'The Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery', resolving to be simply 'Christians' guided by the Bible alone. Two of them, Richard McNemar and John Dunlavy, soon joined the Shakers. In south-western Kentucky, disputes over licensing revival preachers without the usual education led to the formation of the Cumberland Presbyterian Church in 1810.

Methodists, especially under bishop Francis Asbury, adopted the camp meeting enthusiastically, and it became a standard feature of American frontier religion for much of the nineteenth century. Stone's 'Christians' joined with the followers of Alexander Campbell in 1832, forming the core of the Stone-Campbell Restoration Movement, from which the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ), the Churches of Christ and the independent Christian Churches descend. The Cane Ridge meeting house still stands, now protected by a stone superstructure, as a shrine of that movement.

keyMoments.text: James McGready's communion seasons in Logan County, Kentucky, produce dramatic revivals and the first camp meetings.
Barton W. Stone visits the Logan County revivals in the spring and returns to his congregations at Cane Ridge and Concord.
The communion season at Cane Ridge begins, drawing a crowd estimated at 10,000 to 25,000 people.
For about six days preachers of several denominations preach simultaneously while many fall, jerk and cry out in bodily 'exercises'.
Stone and four other ministers leave the Synod of Kentucky and form the Springfield Presbytery.
They dissolve the Springfield Presbytery in its 'Last Will and Testament', calling themselves simply Christians.
The Cumberland Presbyterian Church forms from disputes over revival preachers in south-western Kentucky.
Stone's Christians unite with Alexander Campbell's followers, forming the Stone-Campbell Restoration Movement.

experiences.significance: Cane Ridge is often called 'America's Pentecost' and was a high point of the Second Great Awakening on the frontier, popularising the camp meeting as a vehicle for mass revival, especially among Methodists and Baptists. It reshaped American Protestantism by encouraging a more democratic, experiential and Arminian-leaning religion, and it directly contributed to the Stone-Campbell Restoration Movement and the Cumberland Presbyterians. Its bodily manifestations prefigured debates about revival phenomena that recur in Holiness, Pentecostal and charismatic movements. Critics, then and now, questioned its emotionalism and disorder, and historians analyse it as a product of frontier social conditions as well as religious fervour.

experiences.title: Seraphim of Sarov and the 'acquisition of the Holy Spirit'

place.name: Sarov forest, near the Sarov monastery

experiences.account: Paraphrase of the 'Conversation with Motovilov' (November 1831): in a snowy forest clearing the layman Nicholas Motovilov asks Seraphim how one can know one is in the Spirit of God. Seraphim tells him that the true aim of the Christian life is the acquisition of the Holy Spirit, then grasps his shoulders: Motovilov sees Seraphim's face shining brighter than the sun, feels warmth, peace, sweetness and joy though snow is falling, and is told that he too is now in the fullness of the Spirit.

primarySource.title: Conversation of St Seraphim of Sarov with N.A. Motovilov (manuscript published by Sergei Nilus, 1903)
primarySource.citation: Motovilov's notes, published 1903 in Moscovskie Vedomosti and in Nilus' writings

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Seraphim was widely venerated as a starets, healer and clairvoyant in his lifetime; his canonisation in 1903 was strongly supported by Tsar Nicholas II against some reluctance in the Holy Synod.

assessments.text: One of the most beloved Russian saints; the conversation is a classic statement of theosis and of the uncreated light, linking him to hesychasm.
Admired as a model of Eastern holiness; Pope John Paul II referred to him positively in ecumenical contexts.
Some charismatic writers cite 'acquire the Spirit' as an Orthodox parallel to Spirit-filled spirituality.

The text surfaced 70 years later through Sergei Nilus (also responsible for publishing the forged Protocols of the Elders of Zion), so its exact wording is debated, though most Orthodox scholars accept its substance.

debates: Authenticity of the Nilus-published manuscript.
Imperial politics of the 1903 canonisation.
experiences.story:
Russian monasticism in the eighteenth century had been weakened by the reforms of Peter the Great and Catherine the Great, which confiscated monastic lands and limited the number of monks. Yet a spiritual renewal was beginning, inspired by the hesychast tradition. Paisius Velichkovsky's Slavonic translation of the Philokalia (the Dobrotolubiye, 1793) spread the practice of the Jesus Prayer and the guidance of spiritual elders (startsy). The monastery of Sarov, in the forests of the Tambov region, about 400 kilometres east of Moscow, was one of the places where this revival took root.

Seraphim was born Prokhor Moshnin in Kursk, probably in 1754 (some sources say 1759), into a merchant family. According to his early biographers, he survived a fall from a bell tower as a child and was healed of a serious illness after an icon of the Mother of God was carried past his house. He entered Sarov as a novice in 1778, was tonsured a monk with the name Seraphim in 1786 and ordained priest (hieromonk) in 1793. From 1794 he lived as a hermit in a wooden hut in the forest a few kilometres from the monastery, praying, reading the Gospels and working a garden. Hagiographic accounts say he fed a bear from his hand. In 1804 robbers beat him nearly to death, leaving him bent for the rest of his life; he asked that they not be punished. Tradition also holds that he prayed kneeling on a rock for a thousand days and nights.

In 1810 he returned to the monastery and lived in strict seclusion for many years. From 1825 he began to receive visitors as a spiritual elder. Thousands came, peasants and nobles alike, and he greeted each one, according to those who knew him, with the words 'My joy, Christ is risen!' He was famous for his gentleness, for reported gifts of healing and insight, and for his care of the women's community at Diveyevo nearby.

Among his visitors was Nikolai Motovilov, a young landowner from Simbirsk who, by his own account, was healed by Seraphim in 1831 of a long illness that had left him unable to walk. In November 1831, on a Thursday, Motovilov met Seraphim in the forest near the monastery, in the snow. According to Motovilov's later written account, Seraphim told him that the true aim of the Christian life is the acquisition of the Holy Spirit of God, and that prayer, fasting, vigils and good works are only means to this end. Motovilov asked how he could know for certain that he was in the Spirit. Seraphim took him firmly by the shoulders and said they were both now in the Spirit of God.

Motovilov wrote that when he looked at the elder's face, it was brighter than the sun at midday, so that he could not bear to look; he could see Seraphim's lips moving and hear his voice, but as though from the middle of the sun. He describes feeling an indescribable peace, sweetness and joy, a warmth even though snow was falling, and a fragrance unlike any on earth. Seraphim explained these as signs of the Spirit's presence, citing Scripture, and said that this grace was not for monks alone but for every Christian.

Seraphim died on 2 January 1833 (Julian calendar), found kneeling before an icon of the Mother of God. Motovilov's manuscript lay unpublished among his papers for decades. It was discovered at Diveyevo by the religious writer Sergei Nilus, who published it in 1903, the same year that Seraphim was canonised at Sarov in a great celebration attended by Tsar Nicholas II. Because the text appeared some seventy years after the event, and because Nilus later also published the forged antisemitic Protocols of the Elders of Zion, some historians question how much the text was edited. Most Orthodox writers accept it as substantially Motovilov's own record.

After the 1917 revolution Sarov was closed and Seraphim's relics disappeared. They were rediscovered in Leningrad in 1991 and returned in procession to Diveyevo, where they remain a major place of pilgrimage. The former monastery site became the secret nuclear weapons centre Arzamas-16, now again called Sarov.

keyMoments.text: Prokhor Moshnin, the future Seraphim, is born in Kursk to a merchant family (some sources give 1759).
He enters the monastery of Sarov as a novice.
Now a hieromonk named Seraphim, he begins years of solitary life in a forest hermitage near Sarov.
He is severely beaten by robbers and asks that they be forgiven.
After long seclusion he begins to receive crowds of visitors as a spiritual elder.
In the snowy forest Seraphim tells Nikolai Motovilov that the goal of Christian life is acquiring the Holy Spirit, and Motovilov sees his face shining like the sun.
Seraphim dies kneeling before an icon of the Mother of God (Julian calendar).
Motovilov's account is published by Sergei Nilus, and Seraphim is canonised at Sarov in the presence of Nicholas II.
Seraphim's relics, lost after the revolution, are rediscovered and returned to Diveyevo.

experiences.significance: Seraphim of Sarov is among the most beloved saints of Russian Orthodoxy, and his conversation with Motovilov, with its definition of Christian life as 'the acquisition of the Holy Spirit', has become one of the best-known texts of modern Orthodox spirituality, translated widely and read by Catholics, Protestants and charismatics. The account of the shining face is often cited as a modern example of the uncreated light taught by the hesychasts. His canonisation in 1903 was also bound up with late imperial Russian politics and popular piety. Critical historians question the late publication and editing of the text, while devotees see it as a faithful record of a living tradition.

experiences.title: Bernadette Soubirous and the apparitions at Lourdes
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Bernadette's statements to investigators: between 11 February and 16 July 1858, fourteen-year-old Bernadette, from a poor family, reports eighteen appearances of a young lady in white in a grotto by the river Gave. On 25 February she scrapes at the ground and a spring emerges. On 25 March, asked her name, the lady says in the local Occitan 'Que soy era Immaculada Councepciou' ('I am the Immaculate Conception'), a phrase Bernadette says she did not understand. Pilgrims soon reported healings from the spring water.

primarySource.title: Bernadette's statements and the episcopal commission of Tarbes
primarySource.citation: Testimonies to Abbé Peyramale and Commissioner Jacomet (1858); pastoral letter of Bishop Laurence approving the apparitions (18 January 1862)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Local civil authorities initially closed the grotto; the bishop's commission approved the apparitions in 1862. Many Catholics saw them as heaven's confirmation of Pius IX's 1854 definition of the Immaculate Conception. A Medical Bureau (founded 1883) examines claimed cures; around 70 have been declared miraculous by bishops.

assessments.text: An approved apparition and one of the largest pilgrimage sites in the world; belief in it is permitted but not required. The Church applies stringent criteria to declare healings miraculous.
Orthodoxy does not accept the dogma of the Immaculate Conception as defined by Rome, and so is reserved about the apparition's central message.
Generally sceptical of Marian apparitions; some Protestants acknowledge the reported healings without accepting their Marian interpretation.

Ruth Harris situates Lourdes in the battle between Catholic revival and secular science in 19th-century France (Zola wrote a critical novel, 1894); skeptics note how few healings are certified relative to millions of sick pilgrims.

debates: Criteria for miraculous healing (Lourdes Medical Bureau).
Marian dogma and private revelation.
Commercialisation of pilgrimage.
experiences.story:
In the 1850s Lourdes was a small market town in the foothills of the Pyrenees in south-western France. The Catholic Church in France was recovering from the upheavals of the Revolution and was promoting popular devotions, especially to the Virgin Mary; in 1854 Pope Pius IX had solemnly defined the dogma of the Immaculate Conception, that Mary was preserved from original sin from the first moment of her conception. In 1830 Catherine Labouré in Paris and in 1846 two children at La Salette had reported Marian apparitions that drew wide attention.

Bernadette Soubirous was born on 7 January 1844, the eldest child of François Soubirous, a miller, and Louise Castérot. The family had fallen into poverty after losing their mill, and by 1857 they were living in a single damp room of the town's disused jail, known as the 'cachot'. Bernadette, then fourteen, was small, frequently ill with asthma and had not yet made her first communion because she could not learn the catechism in French; she spoke the local Occitan dialect.

On Thursday 11 February 1858, Bernadette went with her sister Toinette and a friend, Jeanne Abadie, to gather firewood near a rocky grotto called Massabielle on the banks of the river Gave. According to her own later accounts, while the others crossed the stream, she heard a sound like a gust of wind and saw in a niche of the rock a small young lady dressed in white with a blue sash, a rosary on her arm and a yellow rose on each foot. Bernadette took out her rosary and prayed; the figure, she said, passed the beads through her fingers but did not move her lips except at the Gloria. Bernadette called her 'aquerò', 'that one'.

Over the following weeks Bernadette returned to the grotto, eventually seeing the figure eighteen times between 11 February and 16 July. On 18 February the lady asked her, Bernadette reported, to come there for fifteen days, and told her that she did not promise to make her happy in this world, but in the next. Growing crowds followed her. On 24 February the message was 'Penitence'. On 25 February, in front of onlookers, Bernadette dug in the ground at the lady's direction, drank muddy water and ate some grass; a spring began to flow there, which still provides the water of Lourdes. On 2 March the lady asked that priests build a chapel and that people come in procession. The parish priest, Abbé Dominique Peyramale, demanded that she first ask the lady's name.

On 25 March, the feast of the Annunciation, Bernadette reported that the lady joined her hands and said in the local dialect, 'Que soy era Immaculada Councepciou', 'I am the Immaculate Conception'. Bernadette said she did not understand the phrase and repeated it all the way to the presbytery so as not to forget it. Peyramale was reportedly deeply struck that an uneducated girl would use a term from the recent dogma. Local authorities were hostile: the police commissioner Dominique Jacomet interrogated her, the prefect had the grotto barricaded in June, and doctors examined her for mental illness, finding none. In October 1858 the barriers were removed, reportedly by order of Emperor Napoleon III.

Bishop Bertrand-Sévère Laurence of Tarbes set up a commission of inquiry, which examined Bernadette and reported cures. On 18 January 1862 he declared that the faithful were justified in believing that the Virgin Mary had appeared to Bernadette. A basilica was built above the grotto, and national pilgrimages, organised from 1873, brought vast crowds, especially the sick. A medical bureau was set up in 1883 to examine claimed cures; of many thousands reported, the Church has recognised around seventy as miraculous.

Bernadette, uncomfortable with fame, joined the Sisters of Charity of Nevers in 1866 and lived there in obscurity, often ill, until her death on 16 April 1879, aged thirty-five. She was canonised in 1933, on the grounds of her life rather than the visions. Lourdes became the most visited Marian shrine in Europe; the novelist Émile Zola, in his novel Lourdes (1894), portrayed it critically, and sceptics then and since have attributed the cures to natural remission or suggestion.

keyMoments.text: Pope Pius IX defines the dogma of the Immaculate Conception.

experiences.significance: Lourdes became the world's most famous Marian shrine and a model for modern pilgrimage, attracting millions of visitors, many of them sick, every year. The apparitions reinforced devotion to the Immaculate Conception and the ultramontane Catholicism of Pius IX's era, and its medical bureau created a distinctive procedure for evaluating claimed miraculous healings. Protestants have generally rejected the apparitions and the Marian piety around them, while sceptics, from Zola onward, have explained the cures naturalistically, and historians study Lourdes as part of nineteenth-century religious revival and the politics of church and state in France. For Catholics it remains a powerful sign of care for the sick and the poor.
